# Problem 3 - Visualization

## Load data

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(slider)
library(ggrepel)
```

```{r}
covid19_url = paste(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nytimes/covid-19-data/",
    "refs/heads/master/rolling-averages/us-states.csv"
)
if (!dir.exists('p3')) dir.create('p3')
if (!file.exists('./p3/us-states.csv')) download.file(covid19_url, './p3/us-states.csv')
```

```{r}
covid19 <- read.csv('./p3/us-states.csv') %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))
```


## Process data

How many major and minor spikes in cases were there?

```{r}
 daily_cases <- covid19 %>%
    group_by(date) %>%
    summarize(
        new_case_count = sum(cases)
    ) %>%
    complete(
        date = seq(min(date), max(date), by = "day"),
        fill = list(new_case_count = 0)
    ) %>%
    replace_na(list(new_case_count = 0)) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(
      ma_7 = slide_dbl(
        new_case_count,
        mean,
        .before = 3,
        .after = 3,
        .complete = TRUE
      ),
      ma_35 = slide_dbl(
        new_case_count,
        mean,
        .before = 17,
        .after = 17,
        .complete = TRUE
      )
    )
```

```{r}
case_peak_35 <- daily_cases %>%
    mutate(
        ma_35_max = slide_dbl(
            ma_35,
            max,
            .before = 45,
            .after = 45,
            .complete = TRUE
        )
    ) %>%
    filter(ma_35_max == ma_35) %>%
    arrange(desc(ma_35)) %>%
    select(date, new_case_count, ma_7, ma_35)

case_peak_35
```

```{r}
case_peak_35_top4 <- case_peak_35 %>%
  slice_max(order_by = ma_35, n = 4, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(
    label = case_when(
      date == as.Date("2022-01-14") ~ "Omicron BA.1",
      date == as.Date("2020-12-28") ~ "Winter 2020-21",
      date == as.Date("2021-08-30") ~ "Delta",
      date == as.Date("2022-07-22") ~ "BA.4/BA.5"
    )
  )
```

```{r}
daily_cases %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = new_case_count, color = "Daily cases"),
    alpha = 0.45,
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = daily_cases %>% drop_na(ma_35),
    aes(y = ma_35, color = "35-day moving average"),
    linewidth = 1.2,
    linetype = "solid"
  )  +
  geom_point(
    data = case_peak_35,
    aes(x = date, y = ma_35),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "red",
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = case_peak_35_top4,
    aes(x = date, y = ma_35, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    direction = "y",
    nudge_y = 10000,
    max.overlaps = Inf
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c(
      "Daily cases" = "#B8B8B8",
      "35-day moving average" = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Trend in New COVID-19 Cases Across the U.S.",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of New Cases"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

From the plot above, we can see that there are 6 minor spikes including the winter 2020-21 wave, delta wave, BA.4/BA.5 wave. And there is a major spike in January 2022 caused by Omicron BA.1.

For the states with the highest and lowest overall rates per persons, what differences do you see in their trajectories over time?

```{r}
covid19_rate <- covid19 %>%
    select(date, state, cases_avg_per_100k) %>%
    complete(
        state,
        date = seq(min(date), max(date), by = "day"),
        fill = list(cases_avg_per_100k = 0)
    ) %>%
    replace_na(list(cases_avg_per_100k = 0))
covid19_rate %>%
    group_by(state) %>%
    summarise(
        overall_rate = mean(cases_avg_per_100k),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    filter(overall_rate == max(overall_rate) | overall_rate == min(overall_rate))
```

```{r}
covid19_rate %>%
  filter(state %in% c("Rhode Island", "Maine")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = cases_avg_per_100k, color = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c(
      "Rhode Island" = "#D55E00",
      "Maine" = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    title = "COVID-19 Case-Rate Compare",
    subtitle = "Rhode Island vs. Maine",
    x = "Year",
    y = "7-day Average New Cases per 100,000 Persons"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

```{r}
covid19_rate %>%
  filter(
    state %in% c("Rhode Island", "Maine"),
    date >= as.Date("2021-12-01"),
    date <= as.Date("2022-03-31")
  ) %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  slice_max(cases_avg_per_100k, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(state, date, cases_avg_per_100k)
```

Based on the given data, Rhode Island had the highest average reported case rate (37.39/100k) over the full study period, while Maine has the lowest (19.02/100k). And trajectory of Rhode Island was generally more pronounced with larger spikes, especially In early 2022. Maine’s rates were lower and its curve was flatter for much of the period.

These data show a difference in reported case rates. But we cannot infer that the states’ underlying infection trajectories differed. After searching related news, there are [reports indicate that Rhode Island mobilized National Guard members to support testing][1], which may have helped expand testing capacity. While, [Maine reported a backlog of positive test results][2], suggesting that its reported case counts may have been delayed or even incomplete. Thus, these data may not fully reflect the actual spread of COVID-19.


[1]: https://www.providencejournal.com/story/news/local/2022/01/04/rhode-island-national-guard-called-out-rhode-island-governor-dan-mckee/9091649002/
[2]: https://www.pressherald.com/2022/01/19/state-reports-1545-new-cases-of-covid-19-and-30-additional-deaths/

Identify, to the best of your ability without a formal test, the first five states to experience Covid in a substantial way.

```{r}
substantial <- merge(
    covid19 %>%
        filter(cases_avg_per_100k >= 50 / 7) %>%
        group_by(state) %>%
        slice_min(date, n = 1) %>%
        ungroup() %>%
        mutate(substantial_date = date) %>%
        select(state, substantial_date),
    covid19 %>%
        filter(cases > 0) %>%
        group_by(state) %>%
        slice_min(date, n = 1) %>%
        ungroup() %>%
        mutate(first_case_date = date) %>%
        select(state, first_case_date),
    by = 'state'
) %>%
    arrange(substantial_date) %>%
    mutate(state = factor(state, levels = rev(state)))
```

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=10}
ggplot(substantial, aes(y = state)) +
    geom_segment(aes(
        x = first_case_date, xend = substantial_date,
        y = state, yend = state,
        color = "Time since First Case to Substantial Spread"
    ), 
        linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(aes(
        x = substantial_date,
        color = "Substantial Transmission Date"
    ),
        size = 3
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(
      name = "Legend",
      values = c(
        "Time since First Case to Substantial Spread" = "grey70",
        "Substantial Transmission Date" = "darkblue"
      )
    ) +
    scale_x_date(
      limits = c(min(substantial$first_case_date), max(substantial$substantial_date)),
      date_labels = "%Y-%m"
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "Substantial Transmission of COVID-19 in States",
      subtitle = "Definition: ≥ 50 new cases per 100,000 persons in the past 7 days",
      x = "Date",
      y = "State"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
```

Based on [the definition of thresholds for community transmission levels of SARS-CoV-2 by CDC][3], the transmission level is considered as "Substantial" when there are 50-99.99 new cases per 100,000 persons in the past 7 days.
Therefore, we use the first date that at least 50 cases reported per 100k persons for each state in our analysis.
And based on the data given in this repository, the first five states to experience Covid in a substantial way are:

1. New York
1. New Jersey
1. Louisiana
1. Massachusetts
1. Connecticut

[3]: https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7030e2.htm#T1_down
